summary: Defines query parameters that let RDAP clients ask for sorted results and page through large result sets. Without them, server and client processing of big responses can be unpredictable.

plainLanguage.summary: When a search returns lots of results, you can ask for them in a chosen order and a few pages at a time instead of all at once.

questions: how to page through rdap results
subtitle: Query parameters that let RDAP clients count, sort and page through large search results.

tldr.problem: RDAP search queries can return huge result sets that servers truncate, with no way to learn the total, choose an order, or reach the rest.
tldr.mechanism: Three optional query parameters: count asks for the total, sort picks the order, and cursor points at the next page. Servers describe them in sorting_metadata and paging_metadata response elements.
tldr.outcome: Clients can get the most relevant objects first and walk through results in bounded steps, and servers can limit load without hiding data.

today: RFC 8977 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It registered the paging and sorting extension identifiers in the RDAP Extensions registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) has two query types: a lookup returns one object and a search returns a collection. Searches can produce large result sets that servers often truncate. A client cannot learn the total number of objects found, and cannot say which sort order puts the most relevant objects first. It may therefore have to traverse the whole set, or, because of truncation, never see what it needs.

RFC 8977 adds optional parameters to the search path segments defined in RFC 7482. It uses query parameters rather than HTTP headers, because headers cannot be set directly from a web browser and custom headers assume prior knowledge of the server, which the RFC calls a REST design anti-pattern. The listed benefits include lower response bandwidth, faster responses, more relevant results and less processing for both sides.
sections.plainLanguage: Searching a huge library and being handed a random pile of books is not helpful. These options let you ask how many, in what order, and which part.

sections.title: The Three Parameters
sections.content:
All three are OPTIONAL extensions, described with ABNF:

  • count: a boolean asking the server to return the total number of objects found.
  • sort: a string requesting a specific sort order.
  • cursor: a string that points at a specific fixed-size portion of the result set.
sections.plainLanguage: Three switches: how many, what order, and where to continue.

sections.title: Sorting and Paging Metadata
sections.content:
Following HATEOAS, a client should use server-provided links instead of hard-coded URIs. So servers implementing these parameters SHOULD add two OPTIONAL response elements.

sorting_metadata has currentSort (the requested or default sort) and availableSorts, an array of objects with property, default, an optional jsonPath and optional links. At least one of currentSort and availableSorts MUST be present, and a server MUST define only one default sort property per object class.

paging_metadata has totalCount (provided if and only if count was in the query), pageSize, pageNumber and links to the next page. Only forward pagination is described. Servers returning these elements MUST list the literals paging or sorting in the rdapConformance array.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer comes with a cover note: how many results exist, which page this is, and a link to the next one.

sections.title: The count and sort Parameters
sections.content:
count accepts true values true, yes or 1 and false values false, no or 0. A true value means the server MUST give totalCount; a false value means it MUST NOT.

sort takes a comma-separated list of properties, each optionally followed by :a (ascending) or :d (descending); ascending is the default. JSON strings sort lexicographically and numbers numerically, dates and times chronologically, and IP addresses by their numeric value.

The sortable names are friendly property names rather than JSONPath expressions. Common ones are event dates such as registrationDate, expirationDate and lastChangedDate. Domains have name; nameservers have name, ipv4, ipv6; entities have fn, handle, org, email, voice, country, cc, city. Properties such as links, notices and multivalued ones are not suitable. When a name exists in both forms, unicodeName is used if present, otherwise ldhName. Servers MAY offer ready-made sort links.
sections.plainLanguage: Say "sort by name" or "newest first", and the server lines up the answers that way.

sections.title: The cursor Parameter
sections.content:
A cursor is an opaque string pointing into the result set. The RFC deliberately lets servers pick how to encode it, so they can choose a pagination method per user, per query, and change it over time without telling clients. Its examples are base64 encodings of offset=100,limit=50 and of key=example-N.com, but servers are NOT RECOMMENDED to obfuscate cursors with mere base64.

Appendix B compares the two common methods. Offset pagination is easy but slows at high offsets and can return inconsistent pages when data changes. Keyset pagination selects only rows not yet returned, but needs a key field, limits sorting, and allows no jumping to arbitrary pages. A server SHOULD put a link to the next page in paging_metadata, and MAY add first, last or prev links.
sections.plainLanguage: A cursor is a bookmark the server gives you so you can pick up exactly where the last page ended.

sections.title: Negative Answers
sections.content: A request with an invalid value for any of these parameters SHOULD get an HTTP 400 (Bad Request) response. The same applies when the client asks to sort by an unsupported property, or by a property not in the response, and when it sends an invalid cursor. The response MAY include in its body details about supported sort properties or the correct cursor value.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask in a way the server does not understand, it says "bad request" and may tell you what choices it does have.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security services come from RFC 7481. Searches cost more memory, CPU and bandwidth than lookups, which raises the risk of resource exhaustion and denial of service. Operators can restrict search, rate-limit it, or truncate results, but truncation without a way to reach the rest causes inefficiency or decisions on incomplete information.

The parameters help: count lets the client judge completeness, sort brings relevant data first and so cuts unnecessary searches, and cursor allows scrolling through sustainable queries within server limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Big searches are heavy for the server. Getting pages in small pieces keeps it from being overloaded.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content: The RFC says the parameters are feasible because major relational databases, and many NoSQL databases, support counting, sorting and paging operators. Appendix C describes one test server at Registro.it. Its default sort is name for domains and nameservers and handle for entities. It counts with a separate query, because fetching the total together with rows can be considerably more expensive. It uses keyset pagination when the sort is unique or default, and offset pagination otherwise, and it encodes the search pattern and other parameters in the cursor so an inconsistent cursor can produce an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors ran a real test server and found that counting separately and mixing two paging styles worked best for them.

items.title: count
items.text: Boolean. Ask for the total number of objects found.

items.title: sort
items.text: String. Choose properties and direction, :a or :d.

items.title: cursor
items.text: String. Opaque pointer to the next fixed-size portion.
